perspective:
Available to me, John Atcitty:

- I am a Heavy Equipment Operator at the community center. Beverly Yan is my colleague; she teaches adult education and has a doctorate. I sometimes feel insecure about my own middle-school education compared with hers.
- I set up equipment for our joint demonstration and hoped it met Beverly’s expectations. Beverly told me she admired how I handle machines and said education isn’t just about degrees—it’s about what you do with what you know.
- After Beverly praised my machinery expertise, I thanked her and suggested we collaborate on a new workshop combining theory and practice. Beverly said she loved the idea, called my practical skills invaluable, and said we could create something special together.
- After our successful collaboration, I worried I might not always meet the high standards we had set. I told Beverly this. She appreciated my honesty, suggested setting realistic goals, and said our combined efforts—not perfection—make projects successful.
- After our frank discussion, I felt Beverly values my honesty and sees me as a reliable partner, which increased my sense of worth. I told her I was glad we talked and that I could be open with her. She said she respects my openness, trusts my judgment completely, and wants transparency to continue.
- Encouraged by our collaborations and mutual respect, I felt ambitious and proposed a larger community-wide event to showcase what we’ve achieved together. Beverly called it a fantastic idea and agreed to start planning.

I know my own actions, feelings, and what Beverly said to me in these interactions. I do not have direct access to Beverly’s private thoughts beyond what she expressed or showed in front of me.
